title: A transcription factor from the cryptic Escherichia coli Rac prophage controls both phage and host operons
projectDescription: Bacterial genomes are shaped by cryptic prophages, which are viral genomes integrated into the bacterial chromosome. Escherichia coli genomes have 10 prophages on average. Though usually inactive, prophage genes can profoundly impact host cell physiology. Among the phage genes in the E. coli chromosome, there are several putative transcription factors (TFs). These prophage TFs are predicted to control only phage promoters, however their regulatory functions are not well characterized. The co-habitation of prophages and bacteria has led to conditions under which the majority of prophage genes are unexpressed, at least under normal growth conditions. We characterized a Rac prophage TF, YdaT, expression of which is normally inhibited by Rac TFs and, surprisingly, by the host global regulator OxyR. YdaT, when expressed, leads to a toxic phenotype manifested by drastic cell filamentation and cell death. We determined the binding sites and regulatory action for YdaT, finding two sites within the Rac locus, and one upstream of the host rcsA gene, which codes for the global regulator RcsA. The resulting increase in RcsA strongly impacts the bacterial RcsA/B regulon, which includes operons related to motility, capsule biosynthesis, colanic acid production, biofilm formation and cell division. Our results provide novel insights into the host's genetic network, which appears to integrate YdaT in a complex manner, favoring its maintenance in the silenced state. The fact that the potentially-toxic YdaT locus remains unmutated suggests its importance and potential benefits for the host, which may appear under stress conditions that are not yet known.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Two DNA regions, one encompassing racR-ydaS intergenic region (165bp) and another serving as a negative control (172bp, promoter region of Csp231I R-M system) were generated by PCR using biotynylated primer pairs. The reaction products were purified with Clean up kit. 5 µg of DNA was immobilized to 1 mg of Dynabeads M280 streptavidin in buffer A (DNA binding and washing buffer: 50 mM Tris HCl pH 7.5, 0.5 mM EDTA, 1 M NaCl). The cell extract was prepared from the pellet of 25 ml log phase culture of MG1655 by sonication in buffer (50 mM Tris HCl pH 8.0, 100 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM EDTA). Dynabeads were pre-washed with buffer B (protein binding buffer: 20 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT, 100 mM NaCl, 0.05% Triton X100). The cell extract was also enriched with poly(dI-dC) competitor, which binds unspecific proteins. The cell extract was loaded four times in 300 µl aliquots (20 min shaking with 500 RPM followed by magnet separation). The magnetic particles were washed four times with buffer B (20 min, 500 RPM). Bound proteins were eluted with 60 µl of buffer C (elution buffer, 20 mM Tris pH 8, 1 mM EDTA, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT, 1 M NaCl, 0.05% Triton X100). Samples for LC-MS/MS analysis were prepared according to a standard protocol FASP on a 10 kDa membrane. Obtained peptide fractions were subjected for a final clean-up on C18 StageTips following the protocol described by Rappsilber. The prepared samples were subjected to LC-MS/MS measurements.
dataProcessingProtocol: LC-MS/MS analysis was performed on a hybrid Triple-TOF 5600 + mass spectrometer with DuoSpray Ion Source coupled with Ekspert MicroLC 200 Plus System. The system was controlled by SCIEX Analyst TF 1.7.1 software. The chromatographic gradient for the analysis was 11–42.5% B (solvent A: 0% aqueous solution. 0.1% formic acid; solvent B: 100% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid) with a flowrate of 10μL/min for 60 min. Chromatographic separation was carried out on a ChromXP C18CL column (3 μm, 120 Å, 150 × 0.3 mm). The data-dependent acquisition (DDA) analyses comprised precursor spectra accumulation in 100 ms in the range of 400–1200 m/z, followed by top 20 candidate ions per scan in 50 ms in the range of 100–1800 m/z resulting in a total cycle time of 1.15 s. LC-MS/MS spectra were processed using PEAKS Studio version 11 with the settings previously described. The data was analyzed against the E.coli K12 database (Uniprot, 14.01.2024).
